ready2_open_rewrite.final_cot: First describe the image: In the figure, the battery is on the left side, and the current first passes through bulb #1, reaching a junction. This junction goes downward through bulb #2 to connect to the bottom loop, and goes right into a parallel framework: the lower branch has bulb #3, and the upper branch has bulb #4 and switch S. The wire on the right side then connects back to the bottom loop. Therefore, from the image structure, bulb #1 is in series with the parallel combination on the right side/below; when the switch is open, the branch where #4 is located is not conducting, and when the switch is closed, #4 becomes a new parallel branch. Then reason: let the resistance of each identical bulb be R. When the switch is open, the parallel part has only #2 and #3, so the equivalent resistance is R/2, and the total resistance is R + R/2 = 3R/2. After the switch is closed, #4 is also connected into the same parallel group, and the parallel part becomes three identical resistors #2, #3, and #4 in parallel, with equivalent resistance R/3, and total resistance R + R/3 = 4R/3. The total resistance decreases, so the total current through the series bulb #1 increases, the power of #1 increases, and therefore #1 becomes brighter. The voltage across the two ends of the parallel group drops from the original E/3 to E/4, so #2 and #3 instead become dimmer; #4 only newly lights up. Therefore, except for #4, the only bulb that becomes brighter is bulb #1.

raw_record.question_text: A circuit is connected as shown. All light bulbs are identical. When the switch in the circuit is closed illuminating bulb #4, which other bulb(s) also become brighter?

method.method_draft: Treat each identical bulb as resistance R and reduce the circuit. From the image, bulb #1 is in series with a parallel group connected between the junction after #1 and the bottom/right return wire. Initially, with switch S open, that parallel group contains bulbs #2 and #3 only, so its equivalent resistance is R/2. After the switch closes, bulb #4 is added as a third parallel branch, so the group becomes R/3. The total circuit resistance changes from R + R/2 = 3R/2 to R + R/3 = 4R/3, so the total current through the series bulb #1 increases; therefore #1 becomes brighter. The voltage across the parallel group drops from E/3 to E/4, so bulbs #2 and #3 become dimmer, while #4 turns on. Thus the only other bulb that becomes brighter is #1.

method.method_draft: Use node-voltage/current-sharing reasoning instead of fully reducing the circuit. From the image, the junction after bulb #1 feeds all the lower/right bulbs as parallel branches returning to the battery. Closing S connects bulb #4 as an additional path from that same junction to the return wire. Adding a parallel path makes the load seen after bulb #1 draw more total current, so the current through bulb #1, which supplies the whole parallel network, must increase; #1 becomes brighter. Because #1 now carries more current, it has a larger voltage drop. With a fixed battery voltage, the voltage left across the shared parallel branches is smaller than before. Bulbs #2 and #3 are still connected across that same reduced node-to-return voltage, so they do not brighten; they dim. Therefore the only bulb besides #4 that becomes brighter is bulb #1.
